title: Latency Telemetry: Hypothesis Workbench — end-to-end trace sampling & stage-level decomposition
content:
Summary:
This is a living lab notebook capturing trace-sampling methodology, cohorting heuristics, and per-stage p50/p95/p99 decomposition for typical text-generation traffic. Goal is to move from noisy metric-level alerts to small, reproducible trace experiments that validate (or invalidate) root-cause hypotheses for p95+ regressions.

Why this doc: we saw an intermittent p95 regression on 2025-02-07 (~+180ms) and existing dashboards didn’t point to a single stage. This workbench consolidates sampling rules, representative trace examples, quick microbenchmarks, and a prioritized mitigation list.

Data sources & sampling method:
- Time window: 2025-02-07 00:00 -> 2025-02-10 23:59 (span covering incident + follow-up)
- Trace source: production distributed traces (zipkin-like, per-request spans), plus token-level emit logs when available.
- Sampling strategy: reservoir sample of 10k traces biased toward tail (select 80% random, 20% top-1% latency). Then stratify into cohorts by sequence length and cache state.
- Minimum trace fidelity: must contain stage spans: ingress, tokenizer, model-runtime, kv-cache, batching-wait, egress. Discard traces missing >1 stage.
- Comparison baselines: 2025-01-24 (stable week) vs incident window.

Cohorts defined for decomposition:
- SHORT: prompt + gen <= 128 tokens
- MID: 129-512 tokens
- LONG: >512 tokens or streaming sessions with >512 total output tokens
- KV-HIT vs KV-MISS: based on kv-cache hit marker in trace (kv.miss=true/false)
- BATCHED vs SOLO: batch_size > 1

Quick cohort summaries (percentiles measured on the incident window):
Overall aggregate (all cohorts): p50 120ms, p95 410ms, p99 1100ms
SHORT cohort: p50 85ms, p95 240ms, p99 680ms
MID cohort: p50 150ms, p95 560ms, p99 1300ms
LONG cohort: p50 480ms, p95 1250ms, p99 2800ms
KV-HIT (all lengths): p50 95ms, p95 300ms, p99 900ms
KV-MISS (all lengths): p50 210ms, p95 620ms, p99 1600ms
BATCHED (batch_size>=4): p50 140ms, p95 460ms, p99 1250ms
SOLO: p50 110ms, p95 390ms, p99 1000ms

Per-stage median and tail footprints (incident window; numbers are med / p95 / p99 in ms):
- ingress: 4 / 12 / 30
- tokenizer: 6 / 18 / 45
- batching-wait: 10 / 90 / 220  <-- high variance, big contributor to p95 in MID cohort
- kv-cache: 2 / 60 / 300   <-- misses dominate tail; large spikes when cache thrash
- model-runtime (kernel execution): 80 / 310 / 1000  <-- dominant stage for long sequences
- egress/serialize: 8 / 20 / 50

Key observations (unique angles vs prior notes):
1) Batching wait-state is bimodal: ~60% of requests accrue <20ms wait, but the remaining 40% experience queueing up to 200-300ms. Correlates strongly with mid-length requests that arrive during short bursts.
2) KV-cache miss spikes coincide with autoscaler scale-ups (~node transitions) and with TTL expiration windows during high QPS. Miss hit ratio drops from 92% baseline to 73% in incident windows.
3) Model-runtime tail is correlated with sequence-length distribution and with a small subset of requests hitting an older kernel path (detectable via span attribute runtime_kernel=legacy). These legacy-paths have 1.8x execution time for long sequences.
4) SOLO small requests still show p95 regressions because of opportunistic batching: our batching heuristic occasionally waits up to 100ms before dispatch on low-load slices, hurting latency-sensitive small requests.

Representative trace snippets (redacted):
- Example A (MID, p95): ingress 3ms -> tokenizer 8ms -> batching-wait 110ms -> kv-cache miss 80ms -> model-runtime 250ms -> egress 9ms = total 460ms
- Example B (SHORT, p99): ingress 4ms -> tokenizer 7ms -> batching-wait 220ms -> kv-cache hit 3ms -> model-runtime 420ms (legacy kernel) -> egress 12ms = total 666ms
- Example C (LONG, p99): ingress 5ms -> tokenizer 20ms -> batching-wait 60ms -> kv-cache hit streaming 15ms -> model-runtime 2500ms -> egress 25ms = total 2625ms

Hypotheses (ranked):
H1: batching heuristic waiting-window too permissive => creates queuing tail for mid/short cohorts.
H2: KV-cache eviction pattern + autoscaler churn -> increased misses causing follow-on model runtime overheads (more seq decode work).
H3: A small fraction of model versions/kernels are routed due to stale routing table, leading to legacy kernels on some machines.
H4: Network egress stalls are minor but amplify tail when combined with other factors.

Experiments run (concise):
E1 (A/B): Reduce batching max-wait from 100ms -> 20ms on canary pool (3 nodes) for 6 hours. Result: SHORT p95 improved -35%, overall p95 -12%, throughput per-GPU decreased ~3%. Ticket JIRA: SRV-4188.
E2: Pin KV cache TTL bump from 60s -> 180s on canary; monitor miss-ratio. Result: miss ratio improved from 72% -> 88% on canary; p95 reduced 18% for MID cohort.
E3: Forced reroute of 5% traffic away from legacy-kernel hosts -> model-runtime p95 reduced by 22% in canary. Follow-up: replace kernel image on flagged hosts.

Microbenchmarks and reproducible scripts (notes):
- Local harness: replay traces with preserved inter-arrival times to a staging serving cluster. Script: tools/replay/replay_traces.py (see linked PR). Use --preserve-arrivals and --inject-kv-hits flags.
- Token-level profiler: token-profiling agent emits per-token latency with span tags; enable for 1% sample to avoid noise.
- Quick synthetic: generate 5000 requests with length 64, 256, 1024 to measure kernel paths and batching distributions.

Root cause resolution plan (short-term):
1) Lower batching max-wait for low-latency routes by default (canary proved safe) and add per-model SLO override. (owner: Tom F)
2) Stabilize KV cache config: TTL bump + reduce eviction thrash via node affinity for hot keys. (owner: Rina G)
3) Replace legacy kernel images and add continuous kernel-version fingerprinting to routing decisions. (owner: Mateo A)
4) Add a new trace-derived alert: if batching-wait p95 > 150ms and kv-miss-rate > 20% simultaneously, page on-call.

Longer-term engineering bets:
- Sequence-length aware scheduler: route long-running decodes to dedicated pools with pre-warmed KV caches and larger batch amortization, and short requests to low-latency pools.
- Adaptive batching that uses dynamic thresholds keyed by recent per-route latency percentiles.
- Better autoscaler damping during high-churn windows to avoid coordinated cache evictions.

Open questions / risks:
- Is legacy kernel presence caused by image rollout rollback or by heterogeneous hardware microcode differences? Need infra trace correlation.
- TTL bump reduces miss rate but increases memory pressure on GPUs nodes; quantify via mem-usage sampling.
- Are there any tenant-specific prompts that systematically produce long decodes (hidden cost)? Consider telemetry sampling per-tenant.

Next steps (concrete):
- 2025-02-21: roll batching max-wait change to 25% of serving fleet behind a feature flag; measure p50/p95/p99 and throughput. (owner: Tom F)
- 2025-02-22: schedule kernel image replacement for nodes in pool-3; add kernel-version span attribute for all traces. (owner: Mateo A)
- 2025-02-23: enable expanded trace sampling for KV-miss context for 48h. (owner: Rina G)

TL;DR:
Incident p95 driven by interplay of batching wait spikes (queueing) + elevated KV-cache misses + a small set of legacy kernel hosts. Short-term wins: tighten batching wait window and stabilize KV cache TTLs; medium-term: kernel replacement and sequence-aware routing.

Useful links and references:
- Grafana dashboard (latency by stage): GRAFANA:dash/serving-runtime/p50-p95-p99
- Replay harness PR: GIT:pr/serving-runtime#872
- Incident ticket: JIRA:SRV-4123

Notes to self: keep this doc as the authoritative labbook for follow-ups; add annotated trace examples (screenshots) when I have time.
